title: Design exercise: URL shortener and key-value service
summary: A classic design exercise: a service that shortens URLs, redirects for years and counts clicks. The reference answer sizes the system from stated assumptions, chooses a random base-62 code, keeps the redirect path read-only and independent of the primary database, counts clicks asynchronously.

exercise.prompt: Design a service that turns a long URL into a short one and redirects anyone who opens the short one. Links must keep working for years. Give the owner basic click counts.

constraints.caption: Constraints and numbers.
rows: Create a short link (optionally with a custom alias and an expiry), redirect, show click totals per link.
100 million new links per year; 100 redirects per write, so about 10 billion redirects per year.
every number here is an assumption chosen for the exercise
Peak redirect rate 10 times the average.
derive the per-second rates, the storage and the cache size yourself
Redirect p99 under 50 ms from the service's side; 99.95 percent availability for redirects.
link creation may be slower and less available
A full analytics product, link previews, fraud detection beyond a block list.

clarifying_questions.q: Can two users shorten the same long URL and get different short codes?
clarifying_questions.a: Yes; a short code identifies a link record, not a URL.
302, so that clicks are counted and the target can change; a 301 lets browsers cache the redirect and the counts stop. RFC 9110 defines the status semantics and RFC 9111 the caching.

clarifying_questions.q: How exact must click counts be?
clarifying_questions.a: Approximate within a minute is fine.
Readers everywhere; writers mostly one region.
Owner can disable; disabled links return 410.

blocks.text: Every number below follows from the stated assumptions: 100 million links a year, 100 redirects per link, a peak at ten times the average, and a 5-year life for a link. The tables carry the arithmetic; the paragraphs carry the assumptions.

100 redirects per write, so 10 billion a year

blocks.caption: Sizes: the link store, the hot cache and the click log.

100 million records times 500 bytes, before indexes
5 years of links at 50 GB each: one primary with replicas holds it; sharding is a choice, not a need

a redirect response is a few hundred bytes

blocks.text: The storage number is what settles the first architectural question: a quarter of a terabyte after five years fits one relational primary with read replicas, so the answer writes down a sharding plan and does not build it. The cache number settles the second: the hot set fits in memory, so the redirect path is a cache read, not a database read, and the primer's Pastebin solution sizes the same read-heavy shape the same way.

The redirect path is read-only and stateless: an edge that does not cache the 302, a redirect service, a cache in front of read replicas, and an asynchronous click log. Link creation is a separate API that writes to the primary and invalidates the cache. The two paths share the database and nothing else, which is what lets redirects stay up when creation cannot.

blocks.text: The redirect answers 302, not 301, and sends it with Cache-Control: no-store. The HTTP semantics RFC makes a 301 heuristically cacheable, so browsers and CDNs would stop asking and the click counts would stop; the HTTP caching RFC defines no-store as the directive that forbids a cache from storing the response at all. The redirect status is therefore a product decision taken on purpose: counts and the ability to disable a link outweigh one saved round trip.

blocks.legend: The same boxes as the neutral diagram, one AWS service each: the edge is an Application Load Balancer (the front-door decision below says why not CloudFront), the redirect service is an ECS on Fargate service, the link API and the aggregator are Lambda functions, the cache is an ElastiCache for Valkey cluster, the primary with its replicas is one DynamoDB table whose replicas AWS runs, the click log is a Kinesis data stream and the click counts are a second DynamoDB table. Both owners and browsers enter through the load balancer, which sends a path to a task or to a function s8. Each arrow says how the call is made: HTTPS from clients, HTTP inside the VPC, a direct invoke from the load balancer to a function, named SDK calls over the gateway endpoint s9 and the Kinesis interface endpoint s10, cache reads and writes, and the event source mapping that polls the stream in batches s11. Sync means the caller waits for the answer; async means the work goes on after the caller has been answered. The VPC frames are one VPC in one Region across three Availability Zones; the link API function is attached to the VPC through private subnets s12, the aggregator is not. The link API also serves the stats endpoint: it checks the owner on the links table and reads the click counts table.

Edge is the Application Load Balancer, drawn as one lane here and in every sequence diagram below. The load balancer invokes the function directly s8. The conditional writes and the all-or-nothing transaction s13, s14; the SDK retry with backoff and jitter s15; the write goes over the gateway endpoint s9. The DEL is the same cache delete as on a disable; a code looked up before it existed has a negative entry with a shorter TTL, and this delete is what keeps it from hiding the new link.

blocks.text: The rare collision is the design's uniqueness check doing its job: the transaction is cancelled with a reason per item, the function reads which item failed, and a taken code means a fresh random code, while a custom alias goes through the same condition. A request that repeats the idempotency key returns the first code, so a client that never saw the 201 can retry safely. After a successful create the function deletes the code's cache entry, for a random code and for a custom alias alike, so a negative entry cached by an earlier lookup of that code is gone before the owner shares the link. The key item carries a TTL attribute and is deleted by DynamoDB later; the deletion may lag by days, which is harmless because a key only has to exist while retries are plausible.

blocks.text: The cache entry is deleted after the table is updated, never before. A redirect that read the old item just before the update can still write it back after the delete, and that entry lives until its TTL, which is therefore the upper bound on the staleness; the neutral design accepts a stale active link for a short window and states it, and on AWS the window is the table's eventual consistency plus this race.

A task in a private subnet pulls its image through the Amazon ECR interface endpoints and an S3 gateway endpoint (or through a NAT gateway), and this design uses the endpoints.

blocks.text: A miss fills the cache; a code that does not exist gets a negative entry with a shorter TTL, so a storm of bad codes reaches the table once per entry, not once per request. The table's TTL deletes an expired link within days of its expires_at, not at that moment, so the redirect service compares the timestamp itself and treats a link past it as it treats a disabled one.

blocks.text: The service never waits for the stream: events go into an in-memory buffer and a background thread sends them with PutRecords, so a slow or failing stream costs events, not redirects. Each record is billed as at least 1 KB, so a 100-byte event costs ten times its size on the ingest line; packing several events into one record is the lever.
Part c: counting the clicks, asynchronous from the redirect's point of view.

blocks.legend: Open arrows are the stream's deliveries; solid arrows are the aggregator's own synchronous calls. The event source mapping reads in batches and processes each event at least once s11; retries, batch splitting and the failure destination are mapping parameters s28; a stream keeps its records for 24 hours by default s26.

blocks.text: The aggregator never answers anyone: its signals are the counts it writes and the iterator age of the stream. By default Lambda retries a failing batch until the records expire, so one poison batch would hold a shard for a day; the mapping is therefore set to retry a bounded number of times, split the batch and send what it cannot process to a failure destination, which costs a few counts and never a redirect. A batch delivered twice adds twice, which the approximate-count requirement already tolerates.

blocks.caption: The link store: DynamoDB, or Aurora and RDS.

rows.pick_when: every hot-path access is a lookup by one key, the write rate is small, records expire by a TTL, and nobody wants to plan capacity or shards
rows.avoid_when: the hot path needs joins, ad hoc queries across links and owners, or transactions that reach beyond a few items
rows.example: For this design: chosen. A redirect is one GetItem by code, the uniqueness of codes and aliases is a conditional write, the 5-year expiry is a TTL attribute, and the 10x plan to partition by code is work the service does itself. The neutral failure row primary down becomes a throttled or unreachable table, which the cache absorbs for the hot set.

rows.option: Amazon DynamoDB, provisioned capacity with auto scaling
rows.pick_when: the load is steady and predictable enough that reserved units cost less than on-demand's price per request
rows.avoid_when: the load swings, or nobody wants to tune capacity
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. Creations and cache misses are both small, so the saving is a few dollars a month against a throttling risk at the next spike; the serverless lens makes on-demand the default.

rows.option: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL or Amazon RDS, a writer and read replicas
rows.pick_when: the product needs joins, reporting across links and owners, or the team's relational tooling is the asset to keep
rows.avoid_when: the hot path is a lookup by one key, so two always-on instances, replica lag and a promotion drill are paid for a shape a key-value table serves
rows.example: For this design: the neutral design's primary with replicas, and the fit if owners later want reports. Not chosen for the redirect path: nothing on it joins, and the table is replicated across three Availability Zones by AWS with no instance to size.

blocks.caption: The redirect cache: ElastiCache nodes, ElastiCache Serverless, DAX, or none.

rows.option: Amazon ElastiCache for Valkey, a node-based cluster with a replica in a second zone
rows.pick_when: the working set is known and held all month, and the service wants its own TTL, jitter, negative entries and explicit invalidation
rows.avoid_when: the working set is small or swings widely, so sized nodes sit idle
rows.example: For this design: chosen. The 12 GB hot set fits one cache.r7g.xlarge node with room to spare, a replica in another zone covers a node loss, the redirect service sets TTL with jitter and a shorter TTL for negative entries, and the link API does the DEL on a create or a disable.

rows.pick_when: the working set is small or unpredictable and nobody wants to size nodes; data stored is billed per GB-hour and requests in ECPUs
rows.avoid_when: a large working set held all month, because the storage charge then exceeds the equivalent nodes
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. 12 GB held all month at $0.084 per GB-hour is about $736 before any request charge, against about $510 for the two nodes.

rows.pick_when: the cache sits in front of reads by key, writes can go through the cluster so entries refresh on write, and low-latency reads of eventually consistent items are the goal
rows.avoid_when: the design needs its own TTL per kind of entry, such as a shorter one for missing items, or the cached value is not a table item
rows.example: For this design: a close second. A redirect is a GetItem by key and DAX caches missing items too, but a negative entry keeps the item TTL (5 minutes by default) where the neutral design wants a shorter one, and the link API would have to write through it.

rows.pick_when: read rates stay far below one partition's limit and a few milliseconds per read meet the target
rows.avoid_when: one key can be read faster than a partition delivers
rows.example: For this design: not enough. A partition delivers at most 3,000 read units a second, which is 6,000 eventually consistent reads of an item up to 4 KB, and the one-key spike in the estimates is 32,000 reads a second, which only a cache can make a hit.

blocks.caption: The click events: Kinesis Data Streams, SQS, or MSK.

rows.option: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, on-demand mode
rows.pick_when: events are a log read in order per key, a bug is repaired by replaying it, and the partition key can spread one hot key
rows.avoid_when: one consumer needs a work queue with per-message retries and a dead-letter queue
rows.example: For this design: chosen. The click log is the neutral design's partitioned log: the key is a hash of the code plus a random suffix so a one-link burst spreads over shards, and a counting bug is repaired by replaying the stream, which keeps 24 hours by default. On-demand needs no shard sizing.

rows.option: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, provisioned shards
rows.pick_when: the rate is steady and known, so shard-hours plus payload units cost less than on-demand's price per GB
rows.avoid_when: the rate swings, or nobody wants to watch the shard count
rows.example: For this design: not yet. At 3,200 events a second it is 4 shards and the saving is about $68 a month, too little to take on shard sizing; at 10x the price lists make provisioned about half of on-demand, the point to switch.

rows.pick_when: one consumer group, at-least-once delivery is fine, nothing is replayed, and each message needs its own retry and dead-letter handling
rows.avoid_when: the consumer wants ordered batches by key, or to replay history
rows.example: For this design: possible, not chosen. Ten events batched per request come to about $100 a month, and there is no key to spread, but a counting bug could not be replayed.

rows.pick_when: the team already runs Kafka, or needs its ecosystem and retention beyond what a stream offers
rows.avoid_when: there is no Kafka estate, so the brokers would be new things to size and operate
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. Nothing here needs Kafka's protocol, and a stream with no brokers to run does the same job.

blocks.caption: The compute: Lambda, ECS on Fargate, or EKS.

rows.option: AWS Lambda, behind the load balancer or an API Gateway
rows.pick_when: traffic is spiky or low, each request is short and stateless, and paying per request beats paying for idle tasks
rows.avoid_when: the load is steady and high, or the handler keeps in-memory state or work that outlives the request
rows.example: For this design: chosen for the link API and the aggregator, which are low and event-shaped: 3 creations a second on average, idle at night, and a batch handler fed by the stream.

rows.pick_when: steady, container-shaped services that keep connections and buffers in memory and need no cluster to patch
rows.avoid_when: the load is bursty and mostly idle, or the platform team already runs Kubernetes for everything else
rows.example: For this design: chosen for the redirect service, on Arm tasks across three Availability Zones, scaled by target tracking on load per task. Per-request billing (10 ms at 512 MB, assumption) would come to about $220 against about $170 for six tasks, and a function is frozen between invocations, so it could not run the buffer that sends click events in the background.

rows.pick_when: the organisation already runs Kubernetes and needs its ecosystem or portability across clouds
rows.avoid_when: a few stateless services and no Kubernetes estate; the cluster fee and the upgrade cadence buy nothing
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. Nothing here needs the Kubernetes API, and a cluster brings three major releases a year to track for one service.

blocks.caption: The front door: an Application Load Balancer, CloudFront, or API Gateway.

rows.option: Application Load Balancer in public subnets
rows.pick_when: responses are not cacheable, readers are mostly near the Region or several Regional stacks are routed by DNS, and the capacity-unit price is the cheapest per request
rows.avoid_when: the audience is worldwide and the first hop's latency matters more than the request fee
rows.example: For this design: chosen. The 302 is never cached, so an edge cache would answer nothing; the load balancer prices the traffic by connection capacity, about $91 a month at the average rate. Readers everywhere are the 10x plan: regional stacks behind latency-based DNS.

rows.option: Amazon CloudFront in front of the load balancer
rows.pick_when: clients are spread around the globe and the lowest latency to them is worth a per-request fee
rows.avoid_when: no response is cacheable and the audience is near the Region, so the fee buys little
rows.example: For this design: not chosen at the base size. Every redirect would pay $1 per million requests, about $820 a month at the average rate, against about $91 at the load balancer, and the p99 target is measured from the service's side.

rows.option: Amazon API Gateway HTTP API in front of Lambda
rows.pick_when: a function-only API at modest request rates, where per-request billing is acceptable
rows.avoid_when: the rate is high, because it is priced per request
rows.example: For this design: not chosen. At $1.00 per million requests for the first 300 million and $0.90 after, the redirect path would cost about $770 a month, and the load balancer can invoke the link API function itself.

blocks.caption: The design reviewed against the six Well-Architected pillars and the Serverless Applications Lens.
columns: what it asks of this design
rows: observability for actionable insights; frequent, small, reversible changes; anticipate failure

cache hit ratio, aggregator iterator age and the table's throttled requests as the three alarms; rolling ECS deployments and function aliases; the code-format rule exercised with synthetic codes before any id change
a cache node loss sends misses to the table, which absorbs the average rate but not the one-key spike until the cache is back
a strong identity foundation; security at all layers; protect data in transit and at rest

one IAM role per service; no NAT gateway on the request path, a gateway endpoint for DynamoDB and an interface endpoint for Kinesis; HTTPS at the load balancer; URLs validated at creation and never logged with query-string tokens
the load balancer is public by necessity, so abuse is met by the block list and a takedown path, not by the network
automatically recover from failure; scale horizontally; stop guessing capacity

two tasks in each of three Availability Zones, so a zone loss leaves the 4 tasks the peak needs; a cache replica in another zone with automatic failover; DynamoDB on-demand; the redirect path needs neither the link API nor the stream
a table or stream outage costs misses and click events, never creations; counts are approximate by contract
consider mechanical sympathy; use serverless architectures where they fit
an in-memory cache for the hot set and a key lookup on a miss; Lambda only at the event-shaped edges; Arm tasks
provisioned tasks are paid at night as well as at peak
adopt a consumption model; analyze and attribute expenditure

the click counts are the biggest line, one DynamoDB write per click, so cost per billion redirects sits beside the SLOs; a load balancer instead of CloudFront at this size; Savings Plans on Fargate once the load is steady
the counts bill grows in step with traffic; the lever is which links get a live counter
Graviton (Arm) tasks and r7g cache nodes; expired links deleted by TTL; tasks scaled on request count
the cache sits mostly idle between peaks
think concurrent requests, not totals; share nothing; design for failures and duplicates
the link API is idempotent by its conditional writes; both functions keep no state between invocations; the aggregator tolerates a batch delivered twice
a duplicate batch overcounts, which the approximate-count contract allows

blocks.caption: What the picks cost at AWS list prices for US East (N. Virginia) as of 2026-10-16, per month; the sizing is this design's own assumption and prices change.
columns: monthly at 100 million links a year
monthly at 1 billion links a year
rows: ECS on Fargate, Arm tasks of 1 vCPU and 2 GB at $0.0395 an hour; each task serves 800 redirects a second (assumption)
Lambda on Arm, 512 MB for 50 ms a request, $0.20 per million requests
Application Load Balancer, $0.0225 an hour plus $0.008 per capacity unit-hour; every redirect a new connection (assumption)
ElastiCache for Valkey, cache.r7g.xlarge at $0.3496 an hour at the base size and cache.r7g.2xlarge at $0.6984 at 10x, a replica per shard
DynamoDB on-demand: transactional creations, 10 percent of redirects as reads, 5 years of links stored at $0.25 per GB-month after the first 25 GB, which are free
Kinesis Data Streams on-demand: $0.04 a stream-hour, $0.08 per GB written, $0.04 per GB read, each record billed as at least 1 KB
DynamoDB on-demand: one write unit per click at $0.625 per million
Lambda on Arm, 1 GB for 10 s per batch, a batch a minute per shard, 4 shards at the base size (assumption)
the eight lines above; Route 53, interface endpoints, data transfer out, backups and CloudWatch not priced

blocks.text: Two lines dominate: the click counts, because DynamoDB charges for every write and the neutral estimates give a hot link a little over one click a day, so a per-minute sum compresses nothing, and the cache, because the hot set sits in memory all month. The redirect compute is about a tenth of the bill; the levers are which links get a live counter and the size of the cache nodes. The neutral fleet grows 4 times at 10x by assumption, while the per-click and cache lines grow with traffic, so the AWS cost per billion redirects falls only a little.

blocks.caption: Entities.
rows: code, long_url, owner_id, created_at, expires_at, state (active or disabled), custom (bool)
code; one record per short link, sharded by code hash when sharding comes
a code identifies a link record, not a URL: two users shortening the same URL get two codes
written by the aggregator, never by the redirect path; approximate within a minute by contract

blocks.caption: The API.
rows: {long_url, alias?, expires_at?} with an idempotency key
validates the URL (scheme, block list); a custom alias is unique by the same constraint as a random code
302 to the long URL, or 404, or 410 when disabled
Cache-Control: no-store so browsers and the CDN do not cache the hop
reads the ClickCount table; counts are approximate within a minute
sets state disabled; the cache entry is deleted; later redirects return 410

blocks.title: The code space: why a random 7-character code is enough
items: An alphabet of 62 characters (a to z, A to Z, 0 to 9) in 7 positions gives 62^7, about 3.5 trillion codes.
Five years of links at 100 million a year is 500 million live codes, about one 7,000th of the space.
A fresh random code therefore collides with an existing one about once in 7,000 inserts at the end of year five; the insert fails on the uniqueness constraint and the service retries with a new code.
At the peak of 32 creations per second that is one retry every few minutes: measurable, cheap, and the same constraint the database must enforce for custom aliases anyway.

blocks.caption: The two sound code schemes.
rows: no: a guess is one in 3.5 trillion
uniqueness constraint on insert, retry on the rare collision
chosen: shorter, not guessable, and the uniqueness check is needed for aliases anyway
Time-ordered 64-bit id in base 62 (the Snowflake layout: a millisecond timestamp, a worker id and a sequence packed into one integer)
not chosen; it returns in the 10x section as the migration case

reference_answer.title: The core flow, step by step

blocks.text: Redirect, create and disable, in the order a request sees them. The step numbers run on across the three parts.
Part a: the redirect looks the code up in the cache and, on a miss, reads a replica.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram autonumber participant B as Browser participant E as Edge participant R as Redirect svc participant C as Cache participant DB as Replica B->>E: GET /code E->>R: forward, not cached R->>C: look up the code alt hit C-->>R: the long URL else miss C-->>R: nothing R->>DB: read the link DB-->>R: the record, or none R->>C: fill, TTL plus jitter Note over R,C: a missing code is cached too,
with a shorter TTL end
blocks.legend: Solid arrows are synchronous calls with their replies dashed; the open arrow is the asynchronous hand-off. The negative entry with its own, shorter TTL is the Builders' Library caching article's negative cache s5.

blocks.text: Part b: the click event is emitted and the 302 is returned; the event never waits for anything.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram autonumber 9 participant B as Browser participant E as Edge participant R as Redirect svc participant K as Click log Note over R: the long URL
is in hand R-)K: click event, fire and forget Note over R,K: losing a fraction is accepted,
counts are approximate R-->>E: 302 with Cache-Control no-store E-->>B: 302 Note over B,E: no browser or CDN caches the hop
blocks.legend: Solid arrows are synchronous calls with their replies dashed; the open arrow is the asynchronous hand-off. The 302 carries no-store so browsers and the CDN do not cache the hop s4.

blocks.text: Part c: creating a link and disabling it, with the staleness the design accepts.

blocks.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram autonumber 12 participant O as Owner participant W as Link API participant P as Primary participant C as Cache O->>W: POST /links, idempotency key Note over O,W: validate the scheme and the block list W->>P: insert with the idempotency key P-->>W: ok W->>C: delete the cache entry of the code Note over W,C: a negative entry from an earlier lookup
must not hide the new link W-->>O: code and short URL O->>W: DELETE /links/code W->>P: state = disabled W->>C: delete the cache entry Note over P,C: replicas lag a little, so the next read may
serve a stale active link for the lag window
blocks.legend: Solid arrows are synchronous calls with their replies dashed; the open arrow is the asynchronous hand-off. A create and a disable both delete the cache entry of the code; a disable updates the state and deletes the cache entry; the replicas lag a little, which the design accepts and states.

blocks.text: The cache fill carries a TTL plus jitter and the negative entry a shorter TTL, so a storm of bad codes does not reach the database. Creating a link also deletes the cache entry of its code, so a negative entry cached by an earlier lookup of a custom alias cannot hide the new link for its shorter TTL. Losing a fraction of the click events is accepted by the approximate-count requirement.

Redirects need the cache and the replicas, not the primary. Replicas in two zones, cache in two zones, the redirect service stateless behind a balancer that keeps a subset of healthy backends per client, as the SRE book's datacenter load balancing chapter describes. If the primary is down, creation fails and redirects continue: the availability target applies to redirects only, and the design makes that true by construction.

The cache is not a source of truth. A cold cache after a restart means the replicas take the full read load for a while, so they are sized for it: 3,200 reads per second at peak is well within one replica's reach on an indexed key lookup, and the sizing is stated, not assumed. When the cache is full, the eviction policy is least-recently-used over all keys, which Redis documents as an approximated LRU driven by the maxmemory setting.

Counting clicks never touches the redirect path's database. Events go to a partitioned log; an aggregator sums per code per minute and upserts daily counts. Duplicates from at-least-once delivery are tolerated because counts are approximate; if exactness were required, the event would carry a unique id and the aggregator would dedupe within a window.

blocks.title: The hot link: one code at 32,000 reads per second
items: The reads are a cache hit, so the database sees nothing.
The click events for that code would land on one log partition if the partition key were the code alone.
The key is therefore a hash of the code plus a random suffix, so the burst spreads over partitions and the aggregator sums the suffixes back together.

blocks.caption: Cost per billion redirects (about five weeks of traffic at 10 billion a year). Both unit prices are assumptions chosen to make the arithmetic concrete.
rows: Fixed fleet: redirect nodes, two cache nodes, replicas
5 weeks of a fleet sized for the 3,200 per second peak
paid whether or not the traffic arrives
a few hundred bytes per redirect
the fixed fleet is the bill; the lever is the peak-to-average ratio the fleet is sized for, not per-request efficiency, and the number falls as volume grows

blocks.text: Each row names the failure, what the user sees, and what the design does about it.

blocks.caption: Failure modes.
rows: two cache nodes, replicas sized for cold cache
replicas serve reads; promote a replica; owners see a clear error
cache invalidation plus accepted lag; disabled links are rare
retry with a new random code (about one insert in 7,000 after five years of links)
block list at creation, re-scan on report, 410 on disable
counts are approximate; alert on consumer lag

reference_answer.title: Trade-offs and the alternative not taken

blocks.text: The decisions a reviewer reads first, with the option the answer did not pick.

blocks.caption: Trade-offs.
rows: counts and ability to disable outweigh one saved round trip
shorter, not enumerable, uniqueness check needed anyway
one relational primary versus sharded from day one
250 GB in 5 years does not justify shards; sharding plan is written down

blocks.caption: The numbers at 10x.
rows: creation stays in one region: a link is created once and read everywhere
the one-key spike grows with it
partition by code hash across a few shards; the cache strategy is unchanged
regional caches for multi-region readers, read replicas per region
old counts move to cold storage
a host lookup before the code lookup

blocks.caption: Cost at 10x, at the same assumed unit prices. The fleet is assumed to grow four times, not ten, because the redirect nodes and the replicas are sized for peak rate while the cache grows with the hot set.
rows: about $2,400 and about $960 per billion redirects
the per-billion number falls as the fixed fleet is spread over more traffic

blocks.text: The id scheme changes when the random 7-character space gets crowded (at a billion links a year the retry rate becomes a measurable share of inserts) or when a product need appears, such as codes that sort by creation time for the aggregator or a longer code for a separate namespace. Existing codes must keep resolving for their 5-year life, so the migration is additive, never a rewrite.

blocks.title: Migrating the id scheme without breaking a single old link
items: Make the new scheme distinguishable from the old by length or by a reserved first character.
Teach the redirect service to resolve both; the lookup table does not change, since the code is the key either way.
Issue new links in the new scheme behind a flag; never touch old codes.

Publish the format rule and exercise it with synthetic codes before the flag flips, because the risk is in clients and the CDN that assume a fixed code length; flip the flag back if the error rate moves.

If the new scheme is time-ordered (the Snowflake layout), add a per-link random component or an access check on the stats endpoint, because sequential ids bring back the enumerability the random code avoided.

L1: A correct API with 302 semantics, and a code scheme with the collision argument.
A cache in front of a database, with click counting off the hot path.
The storage estimate (50 GB per year, 250 GB over 5 years) derived from the stated assumptions.
L2: Redirects independent of the primary; negative caching and TTL jitter; replica lag after a disable stated, not hidden.
The hot-link case handled as a cache hit, with the log partition key chosen so one code does not make a hot partition.
The 10x sharding plan with a shard key, and custom alias uniqueness handled by the same constraint as random codes.
L3: The question whether 301 is acceptable for some customers, and the product consequence of the answer.
Abuse and takedown as a design input (block list, re-scan, 410), and cost per billion redirects.
Multi-region read placement, and what the service must never do: log full URLs with tokens in query strings.

interview_frame.title: A 45-minute interview
items: 0:00 to 0:05: Requirements: ask the six clarifying questions above, state the non-goals, and say the numbers aloud: 3,200 redirects per second at peak, 32 writes per second at peak, 250 GB in 5 years, a 12 GB hot cache.
0:05 to 0:10: Entities and API: the Link and ClickCount records, the four endpoints, and the 302 with no-store decision stated as a product decision you are making on purpose.

0:10 to 0:20: High-level design with the container diagram: the read-only redirect path (edge, service, cache, replicas, click log) separate from the creation path (API, primary, invalidation). Explain the random 7-character code and why it beats a time-ordered id here.

0:20 to 0:40: Two deep dives: availability of redirects when the primary or the cache is down (replicas in two zones, cold-cache sizing, the primary off the read path), then click counting without slowing redirects (async events, approximate counts, the hot-link partition key).

0:40 to 0:45: Failure modes from the table, the 10x plan (code-hash sharding, regional caches, writes in one region), and the L3 sentence: the interesting decision is 302 versus 301, and it is a product decision.
Context and scope: Who creates links, who follows them, the retention promise (5 years) and the exact click-count expectation.
Goals and non-goals: Redirect latency and availability as the goals; creation availability explicitly lower; analytics, previews and fraud detection as non-goals.
Design: This answer fills it: the container diagram, the data model, the code scheme, the redirect and creation flows.
Alternatives considered: The code scheme (random versus time-ordered) and the counting method (synchronous versus asynchronous), with the trade-off table.

Cross-cutting concerns: Abuse (block list, takedown), privacy (never log full URLs with query-string tokens), observability (cache hit ratio, replica lag, click-log consumer lag), cost per billion redirects.
Review questions the doc must answer: What a user sees in the replica lag window after a disable, and how the replicas behave under a cold cache.

depth_notes.L1: A correct single-region design with an id scheme, a cache and redirect semantics.
depth_notes.L2: Sharded storage, hot-key handling, analytics without slowing redirects, cost.
depth_notes.L3: Abuse, custom domains, multi-region reads, migration of the id scheme.
